title: Learning Style, Forgetting Semantics:A case study of SFT and RFT on Classification Tasks

paper.title: Learning Style, Forgetting Semantics: A case study of SFT and RFT on Classification Tasks
paper.abstract: Abstract Why does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) lead to more forgetting than reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), even when all teacher demonstrations are semantically correct? We study this question on classification tasks where tokens within each semantic class express the same semantic answer in different styles. The tasks share an underlying semantic rule but differ in their prompt distributions and teachers’ stylistic preferences. Using a tractable linear-softmax policy, we derive an exact decomposition of the updates into semantic and style components. We show that, at a common policy and prompt, SFT and RFT have parallel semantic updates but differ in their style dynamics. Starting from a policy with no within-class style preference, RFT with exact policy gradients preserves this symmetry, whereas SFT with a nonuniform teacher develops off-axis style drift along a nonzero task mean under population updates. We use this drift to establish a separation under explicit conditions: for population updates from a common perfectly fitted checkpoint, SFT forgetting admits a strictly positive lower bound over a finite training interval, while RFT retains zero semantic error. Simulations over task sequences support these theoretical predictions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Fine-tuning plays a central role in adapting pretrained foundation models to downstream tasks and enhancing their task-specific capabilities ( Howard and Ruder, 2018 ; Devlin et al., 2019 ; Raffel et al., 2020 ) . For example, instruction tuning on diverse demonstrations improves language models’ ability to follow instructions and generalize to unseen tasks ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2024 ) ; reward-based fine-tuning improves mathematical and coding performance by optimizing model-generated responses against verifiable outcomes ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . However, as models learn new tasks, they may lose previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon known as forgetting ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Preserving existing capabilities while adapting to new tasks is therefore an important consideration, highlighting the need to understand when and why fine-tuning can degrade them. Two widely used fine-tuning methods are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which fits teacher demonstrations, and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), which updates the model using rewards for its own sampled responses. Empirical studies find that RFT often preserves existing capabilities better than SFT ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) . This gap can arise even with correct supervision: Chu et al. (2025) observe that SFT on correct expert demonstrations degrades existing performance under input distribution shifts that preserve the task rules, whereas RFT from the same checkpoint improves it. Existing theories offer distributional explanations for such differences. Shenfeld et al. (2026b) identify an implicit bias of online RL toward the solution closest to the initial policy in KL divergence among those that solve the new task. Balasubramanian and Kasiviswanathan (2026) quantify how forward- and reverse-KL objectives affect the preservation of the old-task component in a two-component Gaussian mixture. These accounts, however, leave a specific mechanistic question unanswered: how does fitting a distribution of correct responses induce errors on previously mastered tasks? The ParityMNIST experiments of Shenfeld et al. (2026b) make this issue concrete: the two SFT baselines, trained on different distributions over equally correct labels, exhibit different retention trade-offs, but both preserve prior-task performance less effectively than RFT. Related language-model studies show that SFT can teach response formats ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) , but that imitation can accompany declines in factual accuracy ( Gudibande et al., 2024 ) . To understand this phenomenon, we isolate the role of these preferences in a classification case study, separating an answer’s semantic content from its particular expression, which we call its style . For example, “4,” “four,” and “The answer is 4” are all correct responses to 2 + 2 2+2 , but a teacher may prefer one expression over the others. In our setting, SFT fits this preference, whereas RFT rewards semantic correctness regardless of style. This distinction motivates our central question: Can fitting the teacher’s style preference alone cause semantic forgetting, even when every demonstration is correct? We study this question in a tractable classification model with a linear-softmax policy, where tasks share the same semantic rule but differ in their input distributions and teachers’ stylistic preferences. For this policy class, we derive an exact decomposition of the updates into semantic and style components, allowing us to trace how style fitting induces errors on a previously mastered task. Under explicit conditions and population updates, we prove that SFT causes strictly positive semantic forgetting even when every demonstration is correct, whereas RFT preserves zero error. Our main contributions are: • An exact decomposition of the update. We split the policy parameters into a semantic channel and a style channel and characterize the update direction in each channel under SFT and RFT. The semantic updates are parallel, whereas the style updates differ: from a policy with no style preference, RFT keeps the style channel exactly zero throughout training, while SFT drifts along the task mean (Theorems 1 and 2 ). • A provable population retention gap between SFT and RFT. Starting from a checkpoint that perfectly fits the previous task and has no style preference, we prove a positive lower bound on SFT forgetting under population updates when the next task has a nonzero prompt mean and the teacher’s style preference is stronger in one semantic class than in the other, whereas RFT retains perfect semantic accuracy (Theorem 3 ). • A finite-sample bound on off-axis energy. On top of the population-level analysis, we account for the additional effects of finite-sample fluctuations on the off-axis parameter energy of SFT and RFT. Our bounds cover both semantic and style components and show that RFT admits a smaller upper bound on the expected off-axis energy than SFT (Theorem 4 ), and the resulting bounds are consistent with our population-level analysis in the large-sample limit. Together, these results suggest that fitting a teacher’s style preference is by itself sufficient to cause semantic forgetting under SFT, even when the teacher is always correct, whereas RFT avoids it because learning from its own on-policy samples induces no style drift. In Section 4 , we provide empirical evidence for this mechanism by simulating the model over multi-task sequences under population and finite-sample updates; the results illustrate the mechanisms in Theorems 2 and 3 and the finite-sample effects studied in Theorem 4 . We also report ablation studies in Appendix E to examine the model’s behavior when some of the theoretical conditions are not satisfied. Additional related work : We provide a detailed discussion of more related work in Appendix A .

sections.text: We use a linear-softmax policy, a standard parameterization in policy-gradient reinforcement learning ( Sutton et al., 1999 ; Kakade, 2001 ; Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . sections.heading: 3 Main Results
sections.text: In this section, we compare SFT and RFT by decomposing the policy parameters into semantic and style channels (Section 3.1 ). We first show that, at the same policy and prompt, the two methods update the semantic channel in the same direction (Theorem 1 ). Despite this alignment, their style dynamics differ: starting from a policy uniform within each class, RFT preserves zero style deviation, whereas SFT develops population style drift along a nonzero task mean when the teacher has within-class style preferences (Theorem 2 ). We then show that this style drift can produce a strict separation in forgetting between SFT and RFT at the population level (Theorem 3 ). Finally, we complement the population analysis with finite-sample bounds on the off-axis drifting energy of both methods under fresh sampling (Theorem 4 ).

Moreover, both coefficients in ( 14 ) are strictly positive, so both population updates increase the semantic margin along 𝐮 \mathbf{u} . Despite this shared semantic update direction, the two methods differ in how they update the style channel, as we show next.

sections.heading: 3.3 The style channel: RFT freezes, SFT drifts
sections.text: We next examine whether SFT and RFT preserve uniformity within each semantic class. The following theorem shows that RFT preserves zero style deviation, whereas SFT can develop population style drift when the teacher has within-class preferences. Theorem 2 (Style dynamics) . Under the setup of Section 2.1 , the following hold. (i) (RFT: style invariance) The RFT updates ( 6 ) preserve 𝜷 ≡ 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\beta}\equiv\mathbf{0} . (ii) (SFT: style drift) For any 𝐖 \mathbf{W} and prompt 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , the SFT update ( 6 ) gives 𝜷 a + − 𝜷 a = η [ 𝟏 { a = a ⋆ } − π 𝐖 ( a ∣ 𝐱 ) − 𝟏 { σ ( a ) = b ⋆ ( 𝐱 ) } − P σ ⁡ ( a ) ( 𝐖 , 𝐱 ) M ] 𝐱 . \boldsymbol{\beta}_{a}^{+}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{a}=\eta\left[\mathbf{1}\{a=a^{\star}\}-\pi_{\mathbf{W}}(a\mid\mathbf{x})-\frac{\mathbf{1}\{\sigma(a)=b^{\star}(\mathbf{x})\}-P_{\sigma(a)}(\mathbf{W},\mathbf{x})}{M}\right]\mathbf{x}. (15) If 𝜷 = 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{0} , the task- t t population SFT step ( 7 ) satisfies, for every a ∈ 𝒜 b a\in\mathcal{A}_{b} , 𝔼 t ​ [ 𝜷 a + − 𝜷 a ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[\boldsymbol{\beta}_{a}^{+}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{a}] = η ⁡ ( ρ t , b ​ ( a ) − 1 M ) ​ ( 1 2 ​ 𝝁 t + 2 ​ b − 1 2 ​ π ​ 𝐮 ) , \displaystyle=\eta\Bigl(\rho_{t,b}(a)-\frac{1}{M}\Bigr)\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}+\frac{2b-1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\mathbf{u}\right), (16) so that 𝔼 t ​ [ 𝜷 a + − 𝜷 a ] ⟂ \displaystyle\text{so that}\qquad\mathbb{E}_{t}[\boldsymbol{\beta}_{a}^{+}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{a}]^{\perp} = η 2 ​ ( ρ t , b ​ ( a ) − 1 M ) ​ 𝝁 t . \displaystyle=\frac{\eta}{2}\Bigl(\rho_{t,b}(a)-\frac{1}{M}\Bigr)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}. The proof of Theorem 2 is in Appendix C.2 . Theorem 2 gives us intuition for why SFT can be more prone to forgetting than RFT: starting from a class-uniform policy ( 𝜷 = 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{0} ), SFT can develop off-axis population drift along the task mean by fitting the teacher’s style preferences, while RFT preserves within-class symmetry. A special case is when either teachers have no within-class style preferences (i.e., ρ t , b ​ ( a ) = 1 / M \rho_{t,b}(a)=1/M ) or task means are zero (i.e., 𝝁 t = 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}=\mathbf{0} ), in which case both methods avoid off-axis population style drift. When drift does arise, it can shift the semantic decision boundary through ξ 𝜷 \xi_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} in ( 11 ). In Section 3.4 , we show that this mechanism causes forgetting under explicit conditions.

sections.heading: 3.4 From Style Drift to Semantic Error
sections.text: We now compare how SFT and RFT retain a previously learned task when trained on the next one. Both methods start from the same checkpoint, which perfectly classifies the previous task and whose policy is uniform within each semantic class. The following theorem establishes a finite-time separation in semantic error on both the previous and current tasks. Theorem 3 (Population error separation from a perfectly fitted checkpoint) . Under the setup of Section 2.1 , suppose that: (a) (Common start) SFT and RFT start from the same checkpoint 𝐖 1 \mathbf{W}_{1} , which fits the previous task perfectly and has no style preference: ℒ 1 ​ ( 𝐖 1 ) = 0 , 𝜷 ⁡ ( 𝐖 1 ) = 𝟎 . \mathcal{L}_{1}(\mathbf{W}_{1})=0,\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{W}_{1})=\mathbf{0}. (b) (Next task) The next task has a nonzero mean 𝝁 2 ≠ 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{2}\neq\mathbf{0} , and its teacher’s style preference is stronger in one semantic class than in the other, after relabeling the two classes if necessary: Δ ρ := max a ∈ 𝒜 1 ⁡ ρ 2 , 1 ​ ( a ) − max a ∈ 𝒜 0 ⁡ ρ 2 , 0 ​ ( a ) > 0 \Delta_{\rho}:=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{1}}\rho_{2,1}(a)-\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{0}}\rho_{2,0}(a)>0 . (c) (Training) Each method runs k 2 ≥ 1 k_{2}\geq 1 population updates ( 7 ) on task 2 2 with step size η 2 > 0 \eta_{2}>0 ; write τ 2 := k 2 ​ η 2 \tau_{2}:=k_{2}\eta_{2} for the effective training time and 𝐖 2 \mathbf{W}_{2} for the resulting checkpoint. Then: (i) (RFT preserves perfect accuracy on both tasks) For every η 2 > 0 \eta_{2}>0 and k 2 ≥ 1 k_{2}\geq 1 , ℒ 1 ​ ( 𝐖 2 ) = ℒ 2 ​ ( 𝐖 2 ) = 0 . \mathcal{L}_{1}(\mathbf{W}_{2})=\mathcal{L}_{2}(\mathbf{W}_{2})=0. (ii) (SFT incurs semantic error on both tasks) There is a threshold τ 0 > 0 \tau_{0}>0 , given in ( C.34 ) that depends only on ∥ 𝝁 2 ∥ \lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{2}\rVert , Δ ρ \Delta_{\rho} , and M M , such that for every 0 < τ 2 ≤ τ 0 0<\tau_{2}\leq\tau_{0} and r ∈ { 1 , 2 } r\in\{1,2\} , ℒ r ​ ( 𝐖 2 ) ≥ ∫ 0 ∞ ϕ ⁡ ( t ) ​ Φ ​ ( ⟨ 𝝁 r , 𝝁 2 ⟩ ∥ 𝝁 2 ∥ − 4 ​ ( ∥ Δ ​ 𝜶 ​ ( 𝐖 1 ) ∥ + 2 ​ τ 2 ) ​ t ∥ 𝝁 2 ∥ ​ Δ ρ ​ τ 2 ) ​ 𝑑 t > 0 , \mathcal{L}_{r}(\mathbf{W}_{2})\geq\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(t)\Phi\!\left(\frac{\langle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{r},\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{2}\rangle}{\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{2}\rVert}-\frac{4(\lVert\Delta\boldsymbol{\alpha}(\mathbf{W}_{1})\rVert+2\tau_{2})t}{\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{2}\rVert\Delta_{\rho}\tau_{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t>0, where ϕ \phi and Φ \Phi denote the standard Gaussian density and distribution function, respectively. The proof of Theorem 3 is in Appendix C.3 . Theorem 3 (ii) implies that SFT introduces errors on two tasks that were initially classified perfectly. The lower bound measures the probability of a region where style drift overturns the correct semantic prediction. This error region grows with stronger teacher’s preference Δ ρ \Delta_{\rho} , smaller initial semantic margin ∥ Δ ​ 𝜶 ​ ( 𝐖 1 ) ∥ \lVert\Delta\boldsymbol{\alpha}(\mathbf{W}_{1})\rVert , or longer training time τ 2 \tau_{2} . Old-task prompts are more likely to fall into this region when 𝝁 1 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{1} has a larger projection onto the direction of the new task mean 𝝁 2 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{2} . Together with ( 8 ), these error bounds imply strictly positive forgetting and generalization error for SFT when 0 < τ 2 ≤ τ 0 0<\tau_{2}\leq\tau_{0} , whereas both metrics remain zero for RFT. This separation is, however, a finite-time phenomenon: under continued population SFT updates with a sufficiently small step size, both task errors converge to zero as τ 2 → ∞ \tau_{2}\to\infty , as shown in Appendices D.2 and D.3 .

sections.heading: 3.5 Finite-sample off-axis energy
sections.text: The separation result in Theorem 3 is established under population updates. In finite-sample training, prompt sampling can introduce additional deviations from the shared semantic direction 𝐮 \mathbf{u} . In the next theorem, we provide a bound on the expected off-axis energy 𝔼 ​ ∥ 𝐖 ⟂ ∥ F 2 \mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{W}^{\perp}\rVert_{F}^{2} of both SFT and RFT. Theorem 4 (Off-axis parameter energy of SFT and RFT) . Under the setup of Section 2.1 , let t ⁡ ( s ) t(s) denote the task index at step s s . Run the SFT and RFT updates ( 6 ) from 𝐖 ⁡ ( 0 ) = 𝟎 \mathbf{W}(0)=\mathbf{0} with constant step size η > 0 \eta>0 . At each step s s , independently draw 𝐱 s ∼ N ⁡ ( 𝛍 t ⁡ ( s ) , 𝐈 p ) \mathbf{x}_{s}\sim N(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t(s)},\mathbf{I}_{p}) , with a fresh teacher demonstration for SFT. For every N ≥ 0 N\geq 0 , both methods satisfy ∥ 𝐖 ⟂ ​ ( N ) ∥ F 2 = ∥ 𝜷 ⟂ ​ ( N ) ∥ F 2 + M 2 ​ ∥ Δ ​ 𝜶 ⟂ ​ ( N ) ∥ 2 , \lVert\mathbf{W}^{\perp}(N)\rVert_{F}^{2}=\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\perp}(N)\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{M}{2}\lVert\Delta\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\perp}(N)\rVert^{2}, (17) and the following bounds hold: (i) (RFT) 𝔼 ​ ∥ 𝐖 RFT ⟂ ​ ( N ) ∥ F 2 ≤ η 2 8 ​ M ​ ( N ⁡ ( p − 1 ) + ∑ s = 0 N − 1 ∥ 𝝁 t ⁡ ( s ) ∥ 2 ) . \mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{RFT}}^{\perp}(N)\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{\eta^{2}}{8M}\left(N(p-1)+\sum_{s=0}^{N-1}\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t(s)}\rVert^{2}\right). (18) (ii) (SFT) 𝔼 ​ ∥ 𝐖 SFT ⟂ ​ ( N ) ∥ F 2 ≤ 2 ​ η 2 ​ ( N ⁡ ( p − 1 ) + ∑ s = 0 N − 1 ∥ 𝝁 t ⁡ ( s ) ∥ ) 2 . \mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{SFT}}^{\perp}(N)\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\eta^{2}\left(\sqrt{N(p-1)}+\sum_{s=0}^{N-1}\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t(s)}\rVert\right)^{2}. (19) The proof of Theorem 4 is in Appendix C.4 . Theorem 4 shows that, even under finite sampling, RFT admits a smaller upper bound on the expected off-axis energy than SFT. The following remark discusses how these bounds reflect sampling effects and relate to the population dynamics. Remark 1 (Sampling effects and population drift) . We discuss the following cases as η → 0 \eta\to 0 with effective training time τ = N ​ η \tau=N\eta fixed. This keeps the cumulative step size unchanged while increasing the number of independent samples. (i) Zero task means. If 𝝁 t = 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}=\mathbf{0} for all tasks, the RFT and SFT bounds reduce to τ ​ η ​ ( p − 1 ) / ( 8 ​ M ) \tau\eta(p-1)/(8M) and 2 ​ τ ​ η ​ ( p − 1 ) 2\tau\eta(p-1) , respectively. Both bounds vanish in the limit η → 0 \eta\to 0 . This is consistent with Lemma B.5 , which shows that the expected parameters remain on the semantic axis for both methods when all task means are zero. (ii) Bounded nonzero task means. The RFT bound ( 18 ) remains 𝒪 ⁡ ( τ ​ η ) \mathcal{O}(\tau\eta) and vanishes, consistent with its on-axis population dynamics (Theorems 1 (ii) and 2 (i)). The SFT bound ( 19 ), however, does not vanish, since the term η ​ ∑ s = 0 N − 1 ∥ 𝝁 t ⁡ ( s ) ∥ \eta\sum_{s=0}^{N-1}\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t(s)}\rVert remains nonzero. This is consistent with the population style drift dynamics identified in Theorem 2 (ii). Together, these results show how fitting style can interfere with shared semantic knowledge even when all demonstrations are semantically correct. At a common policy and prompt, SFT and RFT share a semantic update direction, but RFT with exact policy gradients preserves an initially zero style channel, whereas SFT can develop off-axis population style drift that causes finite-time forgetting. In addition, when sampling is finite, it introduces additional off-axis fluctuations, for which RFT admits a smaller energy upper bound than SFT. We examine these mechanisms empirically in section 4 .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: The experiments simulate the model of Section 2.1 and examine three aspects of the learning dynamics: (1) RFT maintains zero off-axis energy under population updates (Theorem 1 and 2 (i)); (2) nonzero task means and nonuniform teacher preferences induce SFT population off-axis style drift and can lead to semantic forgetting (Theorems 2 (ii) and 3 ); (3) finite-sample training produces additional off-axis parameter fluctuations, even when population off-axis drift is absent; we measure the final off-axis energy, whose expectation under Gaussian prompts is bounded in Theorem 4 .

sections.heading: Teacher parameterization.
sections.text: To construct the teachers for the simulations, we assign each token a fixed style embedding 𝐡 a ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{h}_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} describing how its semantic answer is expressed. A task- and class-dependent teacher preference vector 𝐯 t , b ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{v}_{t,b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} determines the within-class distribution: ρ t , b ​ ( a ) = e ⟨ 𝐯 t , b , 𝐡 a ⟩ ∑ a ′ ∈ 𝒜 b e ⟨ 𝐯 t , b , 𝐡 a ′ ⟩ , a ∈ 𝒜 b . \rho_{t,b}(a)=\frac{e^{\langle\mathbf{v}_{t,b},\,\mathbf{h}_{a}\rangle}}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{b}}e^{\langle\mathbf{v}_{t,b},\,\mathbf{h}_{a^{\prime}}\rangle}},\qquad a\in\mathcal{A}_{b}. (20) Expressions with larger compatibility scores ⟨ 𝐯 t , b , 𝐡 a ⟩ \langle\mathbf{v}_{t,b},\,\mathbf{h}_{a}\rangle receive higher probability; 𝐯 t , b = 𝟎 \mathbf{v}_{t,b}=\mathbf{0} gives a uniform teacher within the class. Figure 1 illustrates such teacher preferences schematically.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We train SFT and RFT from 𝐖 = 𝟎 \mathbf{W}=\mathbf{0} on T = 8 T=8 sequential tasks, with prompt dimension p = 24 p=24 , two semantic classes of M = 6 M=6 tokens each, and style dimension d = 3 d=3 . We draw 𝐮 \mathbf{u} uniformly on the unit sphere, M M style embeddings 𝐡 1 , … , 𝐡 M ∼ N ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 3 / 3 ) \mathbf{h}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{M}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{3}/3) assigned to the tokens of each class, and teacher preference vectors 𝐯 t , b ∼ N ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 36 ​ 𝐈 3 ) \mathbf{v}_{t,b}\sim N(\mathbf{0},36\,\mathbf{I}_{3}) . 2 2 2 The variance 1 / d 1/d normalizes the style embeddings to unit scale, 𝔼 ​ ∥ 𝐡 j ∥ 2 = 1 \mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{h}_{j}\rVert^{2}=1 , so that the within-class logits ⟨ 𝐯 t , b , 𝐡 a ⟩ \langle\mathbf{v}_{t,b},\,\mathbf{h}_{a}\rangle in ( 20 ) have standard deviation controlled by 𝐯 t , b \mathbf{v}_{t,b} alone, here about 6 6 . This makes the teachers strongly nonuniform while leaving their preferences varied across tasks and classes. Prompts are Gaussian as in Section 2.1 , with task means 𝝁 t ∼ N ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 p − 𝐮𝐮 ⊤ ) \boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{p}-\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}) , so that 𝝁 t ⟂ 𝐮 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}\perp\mathbf{u} . These task parameters are sampled once and held fixed across runs.

sections.heading: Training and evaluation.
sections.text: For finite-sample runs, we sample n = 25 n=25 prompts per task and process them in a single pass in random order, averaging over 50 50 seeds that control the training prompts, demonstrations, and their order. For population runs, we approximate ( 7 ) by averaging updates over 10,000 10{,}000 fresh prompts at each step, take 25 25 steps per task to match the number of finite-sample updates, and average over 10 10 seeds that control the Monte Carlo prompts. In both settings, we sweep η ∈ [ 10 − 4 , 0.5 ] \eta\in[10^{-4},0.5] on a log-spaced grid and evaluate each task on a fixed set of 1,000 1{,}000 held-out prompts from its own distribution. We report generalization error 𝒢 ( T ) \mathcal{G}^{(T)} , forgetting ℱ ( T ) \mathcal{F}^{(T)} , and the final off-axis parameter energy ∥ 𝐖 T ⟂ ∥ F 2 \lVert\mathbf{W}_{T}^{\perp}\rVert_{F}^{2} , all averaged across seeds. Figure 2: SFT and RFT under population and finite-sample updates. (a) Generalization–forgetting plane, for finite-sample (dashed, faint) and population (solid) updates; selected learning rates are annotated. (b) Final off-axis parameter energy ∥ 𝐖 T ⟂ ∥ F 2 \lVert\mathbf{W}_{T}^{\perp}\rVert_{F}^{2} , averaged across seeds, versus learning rate, with a logarithmic energy axis.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: The main results are shown in Figure 2 . In panel (a), population RFT maintains zero generalization error and forgetting throughout the learning-rate sweep, whereas population SFT exhibits strictly positive values at every tested learning rate. The persistence of this separation under population updates is consistent with off-axis style drift driven by nonzero task means and nonuniform teacher preferences (Theorem 3 ). In the finite-sample runs, prompt sampling introduces off-axis fluctuations that also raise RFT’s error (Theorem 4 ), yet RFT still achieves lower generalization error and forgetting than SFT at every matched learning rate. Panel (b) gives a complementary view: population SFT develops off-axis parameter energy, while population RFT remains close to zero (Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 ), with small residual energy from Monte Carlo prompt sampling. Finite-sample updates produce additional off-axis energy, which grows with the learning rate and is one to two orders of magnitude larger for SFT than for RFT. The observed energy gap qualitatively agrees with the smaller upper bound available for RFT in Theorem 4 .

sections.heading: Control and ablation experiments.
sections.text: We provide additional experiments in Appendix E to isolate the roles of task means and teacher style preferences and to relax the assumptions behind RFT’s style invariance. With either zero task means (Figure E.1 ) or uniform teachers (Figure E.2 ), the population SFT–RFT gap vanishes, while finite-sample SFT still accumulates more off-axis energy and higher generalization error than RFT; replacing Gaussian prompts by Laplace prompts leaves the results nearly unchanged (Figure E.3 ). We also compare the methods under corrupted rewards and under REINFORCE with finitely many sampled actions, and find that population RFT retains low forgetting in both cases; see Figure E.4 for details.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This work provides intuition on why supervised fine-tuning forgets more than reinforcement fine-tuning, even when every demonstration is semantically correct, through a case study on classification tasks with a linear-softmax policy. We show that semantically correct supervision can still induce forgetting when training also fits task-specific style preferences. In our model, fitting these preferences can shift the semantic decision boundary and disrupt previously learned predictions, even in the absence of sampling noise. RFT avoids this source of interference by preserving within-class symmetry under exact policy gradients from a symmetric initialization. The finite-sample bounds and simulations further characterize the off-axis deviations introduced by prompt sampling.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our theoretical analysis focuses on a tractable setting with a single-token linear-softmax model and a shared semantic rule across tasks. Future work could extend the analysis to more general settings such as nonlinear policies, multi-token outputs, and tasks with evolving semantic rules.

sections.heading: Empirical findings on SFT and RFT.
sections.text: Recent studies compare how supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning affect generalization and forgetting in foundation models. Chu et al. (2025) find better generalization under RL to changes in reasoning rules and visual conditions, while Lai et al. (2026) report less forgetting of earlier tasks and general capabilities under RFT across sequential multimodal tasks. Studies of on-policy and model-generated supervision further highlight the role of the supervision distribution. Chen et al. (2026) show that approximately on-policy supervision reduces forgetting under SFT. Zhang et al. (2026) link the retention benefits of SFT on filtered model-generated trajectories to the magnitude and direction of example-induced updates. In self-distillation fine-tuning, Shenfeld et al. (2026a) use a demonstration-conditioned teacher to supervise student-generated trajectories without an explicit reward function, reducing forgetting during skill learning.

sections.heading: Distributional explanations of the SFT–RFT gap.
sections.text: Shenfeld et al. (2026b) relate forgetting to the KL divergence from the initial policy and contrast SFT’s fitting of an external supervision distribution with online RL’s information-projection bias toward small policy changes. Building on the output-mixture simulations of Chen et al. (2026) , Balasubramanian and Kasiviswanathan (2026) compare divergence-based post-training objectives by quantifying loss of old-component mass and drift within an old component. Their forward-KL objective fits new-mode data, whereas their reverse-KL objective fits a mixture that includes old behavior; the forgetting comparison therefore depends on both the objectives and their target distributions.

sections.heading: Forgetting in continual-learning models.
sections.text: Complementary theoretical work examines how task structure, optimization, and architecture affect forgetting. In overparameterized linear regression, Lin et al. (2023) derive expressions for expected forgetting and generalization error that reveal the effects of model size, task similarity, and task order. For sequential stochastic gradient descent in linear regression with a shared ground-truth parameter, Ding et al. (2024) quantify how task covariances, ordering, and step size affect forgetting. In linear classification with jointly separable tasks, Evron et al. (2023) connect weakly regularized training to sequential max-margin learning and show that forgetting can arise despite joint separability. In an overparameterized mixture-of-experts regression setting, Li et al. (2025) relate expert specialization and routing to forgetting and generalization.

sections.heading: Explicit methods for mitigating forgetting.
sections.text: Replay methods maintain access to earlier experience: Rolnick et al. (2019) combine on-policy learning with off-policy updates and behavioral cloning from a replay buffer to reduce forgetting in continual reinforcement learning. Parameter regularization penalizes changes to weights estimated to be important for past tasks. Elastic weight consolidation uses the diagonal Fisher information to weight these penalties ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ) , while synaptic intelligence estimates parameter importance from contributions to loss reduction along the learning trajectory ( Zenke et al., 2017 ) . For parameter isolation, Mallya and Lazebnik (2018) iteratively prune a network, freeze weights allocated to earlier tasks, and train subsequent tasks using the remaining capacity. They provide complementary ways to control forgetting beyond the choice of SFT or RFT.

sections.heading: D.1 Exact and sampled policy gradients
sections.text: The invariance in Theorem 2 (i) concerns the exact per-prompt gradient ( 6 ). Here “exact” means that the expectation over actions is evaluated by summing over all tokens at the current policy and prompt. When this summation is computationally impractical, REINFORCE provides an unbiased gradient estimate using actions sampled from the current policy. This subsection explains how action sampling may change the style dynamics.

sections.heading: Averaging actions and following the trajectory.
sections.text: If each update averages K K independent action-gradient estimates computed at the same 𝐖 , 𝐱 \mathbf{W},\mathbf{x} , its conditional mean is the RFT update in ( 6 ), while the variance in ( D.4 ) is divided by K K . Finite K K therefore reduces style noise but does not guarantee that every update preserves 𝜷 = 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{0} . Once a sampled trajectory develops 𝜷 ≠ 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\mathbf{0} , the zero mean style-increment statement above no longer applies: subsequent conditional means follow the exact gradient at the new, generally nonuniform policy. Theorem 2 (i) consequently does not imply zero style drift along sampled trajectories. We compare REINFORCE updates with different numbers of sampled actions per prompt against exact RFT in Appendix E.2 (Figure E.4 (b,d)).

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.02437v1 [stat.ML] 01 Oct 2026 Learning Style, Forgetting Semantics: A case study of SFT and RFT on Classification Tasks Haodong Liang Affiliation: University of California, Davis {hdliang, yahjin, kbala, lflai}@ucdavis.edu Yanhao Jin Affiliation: University of California, Davis {hdliang, yahjin, kbala, lflai}@ucdavis.edu Krishnakumar Balasubramanian Affiliation: University of California, Davis {hdliang, yahjin, kbala, lflai}@ucdavis.edu Lifeng Lai Affiliation: University of California, Davis {hdliang, yahjin, kbala, lflai}@ucdavis.edu October 1, 2026 Abstract Why does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) lead to more forgetting than reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), even when all teacher demonstrations are semantically correct? We study this question on classification tasks where tokens within each semantic class express the same semantic answer in different styles. The tasks share an underlying semantic rule but differ in their prompt distributions and teachers’ stylistic preferences. Using a tractable linear-softmax policy, we derive an exact decomposition of the updates into semantic and style components. We show that, at a common policy and prompt, SFT and RFT have parallel semantic updates but differ in their style dynamics. Starting from a policy with no within-class style preference, RFT with exact policy gradients preserves this symmetry, whereas SFT with a nonuniform teacher develops off-axis style drift along a nonzero task mean under population updates. We use this drift to establish a separation under explicit conditions: for population updates from a common perfectly fitted checkpoint, SFT forgetting admits a strictly positive lower bound over a finite training interval, while RFT retains zero semantic error. Simulations over task sequences support these theoretical predictions. 1 Introduction Fine-tuning plays a central role in adapting pretrained foundation models to downstream tasks and enhancing their task-specific capabilities ( Howard and Ruder, 2018 ; Devlin et al., 2019 ; Raffel et al., 2020 ) . For example, instruction tuning on diverse demonstrations improves language models’ ability to follow instructions and generalize to unseen tasks ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2024 ) ; reward-based fine-tuning improves mathematical and coding performance by optimizing model-generated responses against verifiable outcomes ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . However, as models learn new tasks, they may lose previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon known as forgetting ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Preserving existing capabilities while adapting to new tasks is therefore an important consideration, highlighting the need to understand when and why fine-tuning can degrade them. Two widely used fine-tuning methods are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which fits teacher demonstrations, and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), which updates the model using rewards for its own sampled responses. Empirical studies find that RFT often preserves existing capabilities better than SFT ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) . This gap can arise even with correct supervision: Chu et al. (2025) observe that SFT on correct expert demonstrations degrades existing performance under input distribution shifts that preserve the task rules, whereas RFT from the same checkpoint improves it. Existing theories offer distributional explanations for such differences. Shenfeld et al. (2026b) identify an implicit bias of online RL toward the solution closest to the initial policy in KL divergence among those that solve the new task. Balasubramanian and Kasiviswanathan (2026) quantify how forward- and reverse-KL objectives affect the preservation of the old-task component in a two-component Gaussian mixture. These accounts, however, leave a specific mechanistic question unanswered: how does fitting a distribution of correct responses induce errors on previously mastered tasks? The ParityMNIST experiments of Shenfeld et al. (2026b) make this issue concrete: the two SFT baselines, trained on different distributions over equally correct labels, exhibit different retention trade-offs, but both preserve prior-task performance less effectively than RFT. Related language-model studies show that SFT can teach response formats ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) , but that imitation can accompany declines in factual accuracy ( Gudibande et al., 2024 ) . To understand this phenomenon, we isolate the role of these preferences in a classification case study, separating an answer’s semantic content from its particular expression, which we call its style . For example, “4,” “four,” and “The answer is 4” are all correct responses to 2 + 2 2+2 , but a teacher may prefer one expression over the others. In our setting, SFT fits this preference, whereas RFT rewards semantic correctness regardless of style. This distinction motivates our central question: Can fitting the teacher’s style preference alone cause semantic forgetting, even when every demonstration is correct? We study this question in a tractable classification model with a linear-softmax policy, where tasks share the same semantic rule but differ in their input distributions and teachers’ stylistic preferences. For this policy class, we derive an exact decomposition of the updates into semantic and style components, allowing us to trace how style fitting induces errors on a previously mastered task. Under explicit conditions and population updates, we prove that SFT causes strictly positive semantic forgetting even when every demonstration is correct, whereas RFT preserves zero error. Our main contributions are: • An exact decomposition of the update. We split the policy parameters into a semantic channel and a style channel and characterize the update direction in each channel under SFT and RFT. The semantic updates are parallel, whereas the style updates differ: from a policy with no style preference, RFT keeps the style channel exactly zero throughout training, while SFT drifts along the task mean (Theorems 1 and 2 ). • A provable population retention gap between SFT and RFT. Starting from a checkpoint that perfectly fits the previous task and has no style preference, we prove a positive lower bound on SFT forgetting under population updates when the next task has a nonzero prompt mean and the teacher’s style preference is stronger in one semantic class than in the other, whereas RFT retains perfect semantic accuracy (Theorem 3 ). • A finite-sample bound on off-axis energy. On top of the population-level analysis, we account for the additional effects of finite-sample fluctuations on the off-axis parameter energy of SFT and RFT. Our bounds cover both semantic and style components and show that RFT admits a smaller upper bound on the expected off-axis energy than SFT (Theorem 4 ), and the resulting bounds are consistent with our population-level analysis in the large-sample limit. Together, these results suggest that fitting a teacher’s style preference is by itself sufficient to cause semantic forgetting under SFT, even when the teacher is always correct, whereas RFT avoids it because learning from its own on-policy samples induces no style drift. In Section 4 , we provide empirical evidence for this mechanism by simulating the model over multi-task sequences under population and finite-sample updates; the results illustrate the mechanisms in Theorems 2 and 3 and the finite-sample effects studied in Theorem 4 . We also report ablation studies in Appendix E to examine the model’s behavior when some of the theoretical conditions are not satisfied. We first show that, at the same policy and prompt, the two methods update the semantic channel in the same direction (Theorem 1 ). Despite this alignment, their style dynamics differ: starting from a policy uniform within each class, RFT preserves zero style deviation, whereas SFT develops population style drift along a nonzero task mean when the teacher has within-class style preferences (Theorem 2 ). We then show that this style drift can produce a strict separation in forgetting between SFT and RFT at the population level (Theorem 3 ). Finally, we complement the population analysis with finite-sample bounds on the off-axis drifting energy of both methods under fresh sampling (Theorem 4 ). 3.1 Semantic–style decomposition We decompose the policy parameters into a semantic channel 𝜶 = ( 𝜶 ( 0 ) , 𝜶 ( 1 ) ) \boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(0)},\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(1)}) , which represents the mean weight associated with each semantic class, and a style channel 𝜷 = ( 𝜷 a ) a ∈ 𝒜 \boldsymbol{\beta}=(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{a})_{a\in\mathcal{A}} , which captures the policy’s preferences among semantically equivalent tokens within each class. Together, these results show how fitting style can interfere with shared semantic knowledge even when all demonstrations are semantically correct. At a common policy and prompt, SFT and RFT share a semantic update direction, but RFT with exact policy gradients preserves an initially zero style channel, whereas SFT can develop off-axis population style drift that causes finite-time forgetting. The main results are shown in Figure 2 . In panel (a), population RFT maintains zero generalization error and forgetting throughout the learning-rate sweep, whereas population SFT exhibits strictly positive values at every tested learning rate. The persistence of this separation under population updates is consistent with off-axis style drift driven by nonzero task means and nonuniform teacher preferences (Theorem 3 ). In the finite-sample runs, prompt sampling introduces off-axis fluctuations that also raise RFT’s error (Theorem 4 ), yet RFT still achieves lower generalization error and forgetting than SFT at every matched learning rate. We provide additional experiments in Appendix E to isolate the roles of task means and teacher style preferences and to relax the assumptions behind RFT’s style invariance. With either zero task means (Figure E.1 ) or uniform teachers (Figure E.2 ), the population SFT–RFT gap vanishes, while finite-sample SFT still accumulates more off-axis energy and higher generalization error than RFT; replacing Gaussian prompts by Laplace prompts leaves the results nearly unchanged (Figure E.3 ). We also compare the methods under corrupted rewards and under REINFORCE with finitely many sampled actions, and find that population RFT retains low forgetting in both cases; see Figure E.4 for details. 5 Conclusion This work provides intuition on why supervised fine-tuning forgets more than reinforcement fine-tuning, even when every demonstration is semantically correct, through a case study on classification tasks with a linear-softmax policy. We show that semantically correct supervision can still induce forgetting when training also fits task-specific style preferences. In our model, fitting these preferences can shift the semantic decision boundary and disrupt previously learned predictions, even in the absence of sampling noise. RFT avoids this source of interference by preserving within-class symmetry under exact policy gradients from a symmetric initialization. The finite-sample bounds and simulations further characterize the off-axis deviations introduced by prompt sampling. Limitations. Our theoretical analysis focuses on a tractable setting with a single-token linear-softmax model and a shared semantic rule across tasks. Future work could extend the analysis to more general settings such as nonlinear policies, multi-token outputs, and tasks with evolving semantic rules. References Agarwal et al. (2021) A. Agarwal, S. Recent studies compare how supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning affect generalization and forgetting in foundation models. Chu et al. (2025) find better generalization under RL to changes in reasoning rules and visual conditions, while Lai et al. (2026) report less forgetting of earlier tasks and general capabilities under RFT across sequential multimodal tasks. Studies of on-policy and model-generated supervision further highlight the role of the supervision distribution. Chen et al. (2026) show that approximately on-policy supervision reduces forgetting under SFT. Zhang et al. (2026) link the retention benefits of SFT on filtered model-generated trajectories to the magnitude and direction of example-induced updates. In self-distillation fine-tuning, Shenfeld et al. (2026a) use a demonstration-conditioned teacher to supervise student-generated trajectories without an explicit reward function, reducing forgetting during skill learning. Distributional explanations of the SFT–RFT gap. Shenfeld et al. (2026b) relate forgetting to the KL divergence from the initial policy and contrast SFT’s fitting of an external supervision distribution with online RL’s information-projection bias toward small policy changes. Building on the output-mixture simulations of Chen et al. (2026) , Balasubramanian and Kasiviswanathan (2026) compare divergence-based post-training objectives by quantifying loss of old-component mass and drift within an old component. Their forward-KL objective fits new-mode data, whereas their reverse-KL objective fits a mixture that includes old behavior; the forgetting comparison therefore depends on both the objectives and their target distributions. Forgetting in continual-learning models. Complementary theoretical work examines how task structure, optimization, and architecture affect forgetting. In overparameterized linear regression, Lin et al. (2023) derive expressions for expected forgetting and generalization error that reveal the effects of model size, task similarity, and task order. For sequential stochastic gradient descent in linear regression with a shared ground-truth parameter, Ding et al. (2024) quantify how task covariances, ordering, and step size affect forgetting. In linear classification with jointly separable tasks, Evron et al. (2023) connect weakly regularized training to sequential max-margin learning and show that forgetting can arise despite joint separability. In an overparameterized mixture-of-experts regression setting, Li et al. (2025) relate expert specialization and routing to forgetting and generalization. Explicit methods for mitigating forgetting. Replay methods maintain access to earlier experience: Rolnick et al. (2019) combine on-policy learning with off-policy updates and behavioral cloning from a replay buffer to reduce forgetting in continual reinforcement learning. Parameter regularization penalizes changes to weights estimated to be important for past tasks. Elastic weight consolidation uses the diagonal Fisher information to weight these penalties ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ) , while synaptic intelligence estimates parameter importance from contributions to loss reduction along the learning trajectory ( Zenke et al., 2017 ) . For parameter isolation, Mallya and Lazebnik (2018) iteratively prune a network, freeze weights allocated to earlier tasks, and train subsequent tasks using the remaining capacity. They provide complementary ways to control forgetting beyond the choice of SFT or RFT. Appendix B Supporting lemmas Lemma B.1 (SFT and RFT gradient updates) . Fix a prompt 𝐱 \mathbf{x} .
